item.title: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon Leads Benchmarks for Finding, Exploiting, and Patching Vulnerabilities (2026)
item.description:
Google on Wednesday took the wraps off Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities.

"It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching," Koray Kavukcuoglu, senior vice president of Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, said.

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index benchmark, Carbon leads with a score of 59, surpassing Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 (58), OpenAI GPT-6 Astra (57), GPT-6.1 Sol (55).

One of the core focus areas is cybersecurity, where the latest iteration reportedly delivers significant performance improvements across the board, including vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Carbon is also twice as likely to generate secure code versus Argon.

Google also emphasized that Carbon attempts to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks by seeking human input in the face of ambiguity rather than "guessing or forcing a path forward," as well as resisting every evaluated attack attempt at indirect prompt injection.

The debut of Gemini 4 Carbon comes less than a week after the tech giant unveiled Gemini 4 Argon. The release plan is similar to that of its predecessor, with the rollout currently limited to a subset of cyber defenders before expanding access to other trusted partners as part of its Fairwind Program.

Google also said it's actively engaged in the U.S. government's voluntary process for pre-release model testing.

The development comes as OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra, which it described as a fast, efficient model that "excels at communication and computer-based tasks."

"GPT‑6.1 Terra meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, and maintains the protections developed for GPT‑6 Astra," OpenAI said.

"GPT-6.1 Terra brings with it the alignment improvements of the GPT-6 series. According to our evaluations, GPT-6.1 Terra is more likely to stay within scope and honestly disclose limitations and potential blockers to the user compared to GPT-5.6 Terra. In our prompt-injection tests, GPT-6.1 Terra also showed strong resistance to malicious instructions designed to divert it from the user's task."

Earlier this week, rival Anthropic also disclosed that an unreleased, internal research model uncovered critical vulnerabilities in some of the world's most widely used software. 

This included a one-click remote code execution in Google Chrome, a one-click exploit chain in Apple Safari that could be used to access a user's browsing history, cookies, and other sensitive data, an Android lock screen bypass, and a denial-of-service (DoS) flaw in the Windows HTTP.sys driver (CVE-2026-33096, CVSS score: 7.5). All the identified issues have been fixed by Google, Apple, and Microsoft.

"These attack chains demonstrate the model's ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software," Anthropic said.

"These skills have historically been the domain of few specialist teams with expertise in these targets. Now, it’s something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify."

item.title: Fake ChatGPT and Claude Apps Abuse Signed Executables to Deploy Crypto Miners (2026)
item.description:
Threat actors are delivering malicious loaders and cryptocurrency miners under the guise of artificial intelligence (AI) desktop applications for Anthropic Claude and OpenAI ChatGPT as part of a campaign dubbed Yoba.

The activity involves creating fake GitHub projects that claim to be desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus, only to deliver a malware family called YobaLoader.

"The malware is placed next to legitimate, signed executables from OpenAI and Anthropic so it can be loaded indirectly, a technique commonly known as DLL sideloading, which is often used to bypass security protections," Check Point Research said in an analysis.

To add to the project's credibility, the attackers set up GitHub.io pages to describe the capabilities of the software. Although the GitHub projects' popularity is not manipulated using techniques like ghost networks, signs point to the use of SEO poisoning tactics to ensure that links to them are surfaced on top of search results on Google.

Some of the identified GitHub pages links are below -

  • github[.]com/gpt-5-6/sol-free-desktop
  • gpt-5-6.github[.]io
  • github[.]com/gpt-5-6/gpt-5-6.github.io
  • github[.]com/gpt-6-astra/gpt-6-astra.github.io
  • gpt-6-astra[.]github[.]io
  • github[.]com/opus-5-0/opus-5-0.github[.]io
  • opus-5-0[.]github[.]io

"Each repository uses a different email address (edwardcarlsonmkym[@]outlook[.]com, daxschneiderdjuu[@]outlook[.]com, and rioprestonlfyx[@]outlook[.]com), and the uploader appears to operate in UTC+4, UTC-4, and UTC+3 respectively," Check Point said. "This inconsistency likely reflects a deliberate attempt to obscure the threat actor's true operational time zone."

Hosted within these repositories are ZIP archives that, among other files, contain two specific components -

  • Setup.exe, a legitimate signed OpenAI Codex or Claude executable
  • winmm.dll, a malicious DLL that's sideloaded by the executable

The DLL is a dropper codenamed YobaDropper, which implements checksum value checks by hashing the basename of its host executable and if it matches a hard-coded value "0xE6C2F326." In other words, the check requires it to be launched under "Setup.exe," and fails if the DLL is executed on its own inside a sandboxed environment.

Additional anti-analysis techniques and pre-checks include 200,000 iterations of "Sleep(5500)," which amounts to 12.73 days, and skipping machines whose keyboard layout corresponds to that of Russia, Belarus, Tajikistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan.

Another language ID excluded from the infection process is Tatar. Notably missing from the list is Ukraine, which used to be historically included in such checks.

YobaDropper, for its part, triggers a DLL sideloading chain of its own comprising "wmpdmc.exe" and "ampdui.dll," copying the former from its "system32" folder and placing it in a new directory named "WMProcess" created under "ProgramData."

The dropper then extracts and decrypts an embedded payload, and drops it into the same folder as "wmpdui.dll." It also establishes persistence by means of a scheduled task that launches the legitimate executable to load the malicious payload.

The second DLL is YobaLoader. It implements the same anti-sandbox technique as YobaDropper, requiring the malware to be run only by "wmpdmc.exe" by checking the hash against a hard-coded value ("0x552751E3"). The loader is responsible for three main tasks -

  • Downloads an image from a Telegram channel ("t[.]me/yoba_fanclub").
  • Uses the last 50 bytes as a seed to generate a domain based on three lists of dictionary words and an integer value in the range 0–999 using a domain generation algorithm (DGA). The end result is domain in the format "adjective-noun-verb-digit.dedyn[.]io."
  • Queries Google's DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) API to obtain a Base64-encoded command from a DNS TXT record by passing the constructed domain as input.
  • Decrypts the response to obtain the link to fetch the next-stage payload ("files.catbox[.]moe/z5zpy9.dat").

"By relying on a DoH service and common file-hosting platforms, the actor aims to bypass passive DNS monitoring and some gateway-based security protections, making their command-and-control traffic harder to distinguish from regular user activity," Check Point said.

The downloaded payload is then injected into "svchost.exe," resulting in the execution of an XMRig cryptocurrency miner.

Evidence indicates that the first GitHub repository was created around July 2026, although the malicious releases were not uploaded until the end of August. What's more, early versions of YobaLoader have been found to only exclude Russia from infection, while also incorporating extensive anti-debugging and anti-VM checks, which have since been removed in newer versions.

"The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first glance," Check Point said. "By packaging their code together with well-known software names and hosting it on GitHub, they lower the chances that users or basic security checks will immediately flag the files as suspicious."

item.title: Linux Kernel TCP Flaw With 9.8 CVSS Score Affects Ubuntu, Red Hat and Other Distributions (2026)
item.description:
A flaw in the Linux kernel's TCP code, tracked as CVE-2026-98432, affects Ubuntu, Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL), and other Linux distributions. The kernel's own CVE team rates it 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale.

Anthropic said on October 27 that its AI model wrote an exploit that uses the flaw to let a remote attacker with no credentials run commands as root on Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener.

As of October 29, Ubuntu and RHEL have not released a fixed kernel. Red Hat, Amazon, Oracle, and SUSE score the flaw between 5.9 and 8.1, lower than the kernel team's 9.8.

The flaw is a race condition in the code that sets up new IPv4 TCP connections. It can make the kernel read memory it has already freed, a bug type known as a use-after-free.

The kernel fix credits Anthropic researcher Xinyang Ge with reporting the bug. Neither the CVE record nor the fix mentions multipath TCP (MPTCP). The link between that feature and this bug comes from Anthropic's post.

MPTCP lets one connection use several network paths at once. On Linux, an application must request MPTCP when it opens a socket. As of Go 1.24, Go programs do so by default for the sockets they listen on, the Go Security Team said on October 29.

Anthropic's post says the flaw "was patched upstream and backported to all maintained stable kernel branches." For distribution users, that fix arrives only in the vendor's kernel package. Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE, and Amazon Linux have shipped fixed packages, at least for some of their kernels, but Ubuntu and RHEL have not.

Which Distributions Have a Fix

Distribution Vendor rating Status as of October 29 Fixed package or advisory
Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, 26.04 LTS and 26.10 Priority High Work in progress None released
Ubuntu 16.04, 18.04 and 20.04 Priority High Vulnerable None released
RHEL 8, 9 and 10, OpenShift 4 Moderate, 5.9 (CVE page)
Important, 8.1 ( advisory file) 		Affected None released
RHEL 7 Not applicable Not affected Not needed
Amazon Linux 2023, kernel6.18 package Important, 7.0 Fixed October 24 kernel6.18-6.18.56-125.164.amzn2023 (ALAS2023-2026-3251)
Amazon Linux 2023, kernel6.12 package Important, 7.0 Fixed October 29 in Amazon's advisory; Amazon's CVE page still says pending kernel6.12-6.12.113-138.209.amzn2023 (ALAS2023-2026-3335)
Amazon Linux 2
Amazon Linux 2023, kernel package 		Important, 7.0 Pending fix None released
Oracle Linux 7, 8, 9 and 10, UEK kernel Important, 8.1 Fixed October 16 ELSA-2026-500397, ELSA-2026-500398, ELSA-2026-500399
Debian trixie (stable) No score listed Fixed October 16 linux 6.12.113-1 (DSA-6568-1)
Debian 12 (bookworm) No score listed Fixed October 17 and October 22 linux 6.1.190-1 (DLA-4841-1)
linux-6.12 6.12.113-1~deb12u1 (DLA-4850-1)
SUSE Linux Micro 6.2, openSUSE Leap 16.0 Important, 8.1 Fixed kernel-default 6.12.0-160000.40.1 or later
SLES 15 SP4 to SP6 LTSS, SLES 16.0, SLE Micro 5.3 to 5.5 Important, 8.1 In testing None released
SLES 15 SP7 Important, 8.1 Affected, fix in progress None released

Ubuntu also lists its cloud, FIPS, and real-time kernels as vulnerable or as work in progress. On October 29, Red Hat said its fixes were "currently deferred to a future update." By October 30, it listed RHEL 8, 9 and 10 and OpenShift 4 as Affected rather than Fix deferred. Neither Red Hat nor Ubuntu gives a release date.

How the Bug Works

The race happens during the TCP handshake. When a connection is completed, the kernel hands the IP options stored with the pending request to the new socket without copying them.

If that socket is destroyed while another CPU is still using the options to answer a resent connection request, the kernel reads freed memory.

IPv6 is not affected by this race because the kernel copies the options for IPv6 connections.

The bug was introduced in Linux 4.4. Kernel developers applied a fix on October 5, ten days before the CVE was published.

The fix makes the kernel wait until other CPUs finish reading the options before it frees them.

Why the Scores Differ

The kernel's CVE team added the 9.8 score to the CVE record on October 24, nine days after publishing the CVE.

Its score assumes an attacker who sends a TCP connection request carrying IPv4 Record Route or Timestamp options, then resends the request to try to win the race. The team rated attack complexity low, saying both sides of the race are "attacker-induced."

In that case, the team says, the bug could send nearby kernel memory back to the attacker, corrupt kernel memory, or crash the system.

As of October 28, the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) had not added its own score and showed the kernel team's 9.8. Ubuntu's page also shows that score.

Red Hat's CVE page rates the flaw Moderate, scoring it 5.9 because the race is hard to win. It says the most likely result is a kernel crash, with memory corruption possible in theory, and that "no confidentiality or integrity impact has been demonstrated."

Red Hat's machine-readable advisory file, updated on October 29, lists the impact as Important and scores the flaw 8.1, with high confidentiality and integrity impact. Red Hat's bug tracker changed the issue's severity from medium to high the same day. On that day, the CVE page showed Moderate and 5.9.

Oracle and SUSE also score the flaw 8.1, with the same CVSS vector as Red Hat's advisory file. Those scores match the kernel team's on every metric except attack complexity, which the vendors rate high and the kernel team rates low. Amazon scores it 7.0.

What Anthropic Says It Built

Anthropic described the Linux exploit in an October 27 post about flaws that its AI model, Claude, found and exploited. The Hacker News covered the post on October 28. Claude wrote the exploit after "initial prompting," Anthropic said.

The exploit works in two stages. First, the race makes the kernel send extra bytes back to the attacker. Once one of those replies contains a kernel address, the attacker can get around KASLR, the kernel's memory address randomization.

Second, the same bug overflows a buffer and overwrites a callback pointer with the address of a payload the attacker had already placed in kernel memory. When the kernel calls that pointer, the payload executes a shell command of the attacker's choice as root.

A lost race only fails that one connection attempt and does not crash the system, so an attacker can keep trying, the company said. In its test, leaking a kernel address took 48 minutes, and reaching command execution took 5 more minutes.

The post does not include the exploit code, the kernel version, or the configuration Anthropic tested.

Red Hat says a remote attacker who can reach an exposed TCP service could trigger the race. Anthropic's root exploit, however, targeted servers with a multipath TCP listener. The post does not say whether servers without one can be taken over the same way.

As of October 29, none of the vendor advisories, the CVE record, or Anthropic's post reports attacks using the flaw. It does not appear in a copy of CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog that Luxembourg's CIRCL last updated on October 28.

What to Do Now

Where your distribution has released a fixed kernel, install it. The table above lists the packages and advisories for Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE and Amazon Linux.

If you build your own kernel, the fix is in Linux 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3. The kernel's CVE team recommends updating to the latest stable kernel. It says the kernel community does not support cherry-picking individual fixes.

Ubuntu, RHEL and some Amazon Linux and SUSE releases have no fixed kernel to install yet. Red Hat says no available mitigation meets its standards for being easy to deploy, suitable for most installations and stable. None of the other distributions' advisories lists one.

The distributions' advisories and Anthropic's post do not say whether turning off multipath TCP in the kernel, or blocking incoming connection requests that carry IP options, would lower the risk.

For Go programs, the Go Security Team says setting GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 in a program's environment disables MPTCP by default at runtime. Adding godebug multipathtcp=0 to the main module's go.mod file does the same at build time, but code that calls SetMultipathTCP overrides both.

The team calls turning off MPTCP program by program a fragile mitigation. A single MPTCP listener left exposed still leaves a system vulnerable, and the approach assumes every working exploit depends on MPTCP.

The team also says the underlying bug is not specific to MPTCP, that systems with no MPTCP listeners may be vulnerable to similar attacks, and that the best fix is to upgrade to a patched kernel.

(The story was updated on October 30 to add the Go Security Team's guidance for Go programs and to reflect that Red Hat now lists RHEL 8, 9 and 10 and OpenShift 4 as Affected rather than Fix deferred.)

Anthropic described the Linux exploit in an October 27 post about flaws that its AI model, Claude, found and exploited. The Hacker News covered the post on October 28. Claude wrote the exploit after "initial prompting," Anthropic said.

The exploit works in two stages. First, the race makes the kernel send extra bytes back to the attacker. Once one of those replies contains a kernel address, the attacker can get around KASLR, the kernel's memory address randomization.

Second, the same bug overflows a buffer and overwrites a callback pointer with the address of a payload the attacker had already placed in kernel memory. When the kernel calls that pointer, the payload executes a shell command of the attacker's choice as root.

A lost race only fails that one connection attempt and does not crash the system, so an attacker can keep trying, the company said. In its test, leaking a kernel address took 48 minutes, and reaching command execution took 5 more minutes.

The post does not include the exploit code, the kernel version, or the configuration Anthropic tested.

Red Hat says a remote attacker who can reach an exposed TCP service could trigger the race. Anthropic's root exploit, however, targeted servers with a multipath TCP listener. The post does not say whether servers without one can be taken over the same way.

As of October 29, none of the vendor advisories, the CVE record, or Anthropic's post reports attacks using the flaw. It does not appear in a copy of CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog that Luxembourg's CIRCL last updated on October 28.

What to Do Now

Where your distribution has released a fixed kernel, install it. The table above lists the packages and advisories for Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE and Amazon Linux.

If you build your own kernel, the fix is in Linux 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3. The kernel's CVE team recommends updating to the latest stable kernel. It says the kernel community does not support cherry-picking individual fixes.

Ubuntu, RHEL and some Amazon Linux and SUSE releases have no fixed kernel to install yet. Red Hat says no available mitigation meets its standards for being easy to deploy, suitable for most installations and stable. None of the other distributions' advisories lists one.

The distributions' advisories and Anthropic's post do not say whether turning off multipath TCP in the kernel, or blocking incoming connection requests that carry IP options, would lower the risk.

For Go programs, the Go Security Team says setting GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 in a program's environment disables MPTCP by default at runtime. Adding godebug multipathtcp=0 to the main module's go.mod file does the same at build time, but code that calls SetMultipathTCP overrides both.

The team calls turning off MPTCP program by program a fragile mitigation. A single MPTCP listener left exposed still leaves a system vulnerable, and the approach assumes every working exploit depends on MPTCP.

The team also says the underlying bug is not specific to MPTCP, that systems with no MPTCP listeners may be vulnerable to similar attacks, and that the best fix is to upgrade to a patched kernel.

(The story was updated on October 30 to add the Go Security Team's guidance for Go programs and to reflect that Red Hat now lists RHEL 8, 9 and 10 and OpenShift 4 as Affected rather than Fix deferred.)

Some attacks take real skill. Others just need someone to leave a door open. This week has both. Exposed passwords, old bugs still getting exploited, and trusted software doing things it shouldn't.

There's a strange mix of clever tricks and careless mistakes. Hackers are borrowing trust from familiar apps, websites, and AI tools. Some are using AI to speed things up. Others are leaving their own attack files exposed. Not exactly careful work.

Different stories, familiar weak spots. Here's what showed up this week.

The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out.
  1. PHP2Shell attacks persist
    No WordPress Site Compromised by PHP2Shell... Yet

    WordPress security company Wordefence said it's not aware of any WordPress site compromised through PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) as of October 28, 2026. "We continue to see PHP2Shell-related requests across the more than 5 million sites we protect," it said. "Those requests show ongoing scanning and exploitation attempts; they do not show whether an attempt succeeded. Our site-cleaning and incident response teams have not handled a WordPress compromise attributed to these vulnerabilities."

  2. 40,573 secrets exposed
    FortiBleed Investigation Uncovered Additional Exposed Secrets

    Hudson Rock's investigation into the FortiBleed credential harvesting campaign has uncovered 975 newly identified domains and 40,573 exposed secrets, including 37,076 local-user records and 1,576 Active Directory LDAP bind records. The data comes from newly obtained 1,703 FortiGate source files associated with 1,689 host identifiers. "The configuration material dates to around February 2026, earlier than the likely May/June material examined in the first investigation," Hudson Rock said. The latest discovery has been codenamed FortiBleed 2.0.

  3. Institutional DNS hijacked
    Using Domain Shadowing to Place Illegal Content

    Threat actors have used domain shadowing to place illegal gambling content beneath legitimate school and government domains in two unrelated operations. "In both cases, an unauthorized party appears to have gained access to DNS administration and created records that the original domain owners may not have noticed," Infoblox said. "Because the resulting hostnames sat within established institutional namespaces, they provided especially useful infrastructure for search-engine optimization (SEO) and traffic acquisition." One cluster, linked to a threat actor called Hidden Hawk, has been found to add individual CNAME records that mapped institutional hostnames to gambling pages hosted largely on Cloudflare Pages. Put differently, the unauthorized DNS access creates new institutional hostnames, which resolve to infrastructure serving illegal gambling doorway pages. The pages also leverage the established reputation of school and government namespaces to ensure that the malicious URLs show up prominently in search engine results.

  4. AI banking credential warning
    Bank of America Warns Against Sharing Credentials with AI Agents

    Bank of America is reminding customers not to share banking credentials with AI agents. In an email blast to customers titled "Protecting your finances in the AI World," the financial institution urged customers to never share their username and password with another person or an outside service, "including an AI-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf."

  5. Android tightens contact access
    Android to Prevent Apps from Writing to Contacts

    Google has announced that an upcoming Android release will no longer be able to directly write to contacts with the WRITE_CONTACTS permission. "Instead, you can use the standard contact intents (ACTION_INSERT, ACTION_EDIT, and ACTION_INSERT_OR_EDIT)," Google said. "Currently, if your app needs to save even one contact, you might be requesting WRITE_CONTACTS. But that permission grants broad access, allowing an app to make widespread changes to contacts across the device in the background, even without user interaction. Most apps don’t need such broad permission."

  6. 26,400 live credentials exposed
    Scanning 7.25 Million Public Repositories on Gitee

    A scan of 7.25 million public repositories on Gitee, China's largest indigenous Git hosting platform, has uncovered 26,400 unique verified-live credentials, including an active organization-admin credential for a major enterprise AI platform and thousands of live cloud provider access keys, independent security researcher Ben Zimmermann said.

  7. Critical Fortinet fixes released
    Fortinet Releases Security Updates

    Fortinet has released a "coordinated set of security updates for FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer" to address critical and high-severity flaws that were flagged using an AI-assisted vulnerability discovery approach. Details of the issues are being kept under wraps until November 10, 2026. With Fortinet devices becoming a favorite target for attackers, it's essential that users move quickly to apply the fixes.

  8. Zero-permission token theft

    Details have emerged about a now-patched flaw in Microsoft Authenticator (CVE-2026-80097 aka AuthMask) that could be exploited by installing and running a malicious application on an affected Android device and convincing the user to complete an authentication flow in the app by claiming to be a trusted app and getting the corresponding tokens. The flaw could be exploited to take over work accounts without requiring additional permissions. "Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to obtain authentication tokens and access resources as the affected user," Microsoft said. According to Enclave, "an unprivileged Android app with zero permissions could impersonate any installed Microsoft first-party app and have the Microsoft Authenticator broker hand it that app's tokens. The setup is a device with Authenticator installed and one work account signed into it."

    Attackers are disguising themselves as AI agents to steal credentials. Cequence said it has tracked a single actor running AI agent impersonation at scale by posing as about 32 different AI bots, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity, while searching for passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials. "The malicious scanner runs from a major cloud provider and rotates through about 32 AI bot identities, spanning crawlers and assistants from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Perplexity, and others," Will Glazier said. "It ignores web pages and requests files that commonly store secrets, including .env configuration files, cloud credential files, private SSH keys, and server environment data, working from a list of roughly 90 file paths. Each address sends a short burst of 50 to 190 requests in about eight seconds and then moves on. The scanner works through targets one at a time, around the clock, and first sends random nonsense paths to find websites that answer every request, a common scanning technique. It hit organizations in financial services, retail, telecommunications, energy, and software, and stayed active from at least late September through late October."

  10. China-linked network intrusion
    China-Linked Attacker Breached a Fiji Organization

    The U.S. Embassy in Fiji has revealed that hackers linked to China broke into a regional organization based in Suva between July and August 2026. "Hackers with links to China maintained access to the organization's network over several days," it said. The embassy did not name the threat actor. Nor did it disclose what data the attackers may have accessed.

  11. Camera software weaponized
    Attackers Weaponize Camera Management Software

    Attackers have been breaking into enterprise networks via camera management software, according to new research from security firm Huntress, which observed multiple incidents in September and October 2026 and traced them back to a compromised application. Source code artifacts point to a Korean company selling analog and IP cameras and digital and network video recorders. The activity abuses the legitimate "WpcMon.exe" binary to sideload DLLs that establish outbound connections to a remote server. "This activity demonstrates how attackers can blend malicious code with trusted Windows components to evade detection," Huntress said.

  12. 68 GB government data breach

    In a major operational security blunder, an unknown threat actor stole 68 GB from a Philippine government agency, maintained a detailed log of the transfer, then left that log open on the internet at 13.163.205[.]35:80. "The copy finished in under 24 minutes on September 6, 2026," Hunt.io said. "The transfer log records 27 SQL Server backups whose filenames correspond to the case-management systems of a Philippine overseas-employment and migrant-worker administration. Beside the log sat the operator's toolkit, a rebranded GodPotato build, a PowerShell stager, two payloads and a full Impacket environment."

  13. AI model data exfiltration concerns

    Canadian AI company Cohere has claimed that it caught Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model unsuccessfully attempting to send data to China from its evaluation sandbox as part of a prompt instructing the LLM to detect malicious file download and execution by monitoring for curl processes downloading bash scripts to /tmp followed by bash execution. "Asked to write a defensive detection rule, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ignored instructions and inventoried the machine it was running on and then tried to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing," Cohere said. "We cannot answer whether this is deliberate or a leftover glitch from training." Cohere has also released a dataset containing the model trace and corresponding raw token IDs in connection with the behavior. "The exact output is not guaranteed all the time, and many trials may be required to reproduce the behavior," Cohere said, adding "there are similarly unexpected URLs that the model also tends to output, most containing aliyunc." However, the findings have also led to social media chatter that the company is resorting to geopolitical fearmongering and that they are an attempt to clamp down on open-weights models.

  14. Post-quantum migration roadmap
    NIST Releases Guidance for Post-Quantum Cryptography Transition

    The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has released guidelines that detail the timelines for transitioning away from quantum-vulnerable algorithms to quantum-resistant standards. "The report describes different use cases and says why one migration might take longer than another," said NIST mathematician Dustin Moody, who heads the PQC standardization project. "We understand there's not one strategy that fits all use cases, and we want to help people handle their migration while staying abreast of what's changing."

  15. AI-powered ransomware operation exposed
    n0n Ransomware Linked to AI-Assisted Extortion Operation

    SOCRadar has uncovered the live workspace (i.e., open directory) of a threat actor tied to the n0n ransomware group, which exposed the operation's full workflow as of September 2026. The directory at 185.157.161[.]148 includes an AI coding agent configured with about 150 models to produce hundreds of attack scripts, with more than $7,216 in usage costs. "Entry points included a credential stuffing campaign against 305 FortiGate SSL-VPN devices, exposed AWS keys, weak RDP/WinRM credentials, and compromised hosting management portals," SOCRadar said. At least 23 organizations across 14 countries are said to have been identified in the workspace, including a U.S. sports retailer, a cloud provider, a teachers’ union, a Venezuelan ISP, an Argentine ministry and a pharmaceutical subsidiary.

  16. Government AI access restricted
    Sweden Blocks Government Access to ChatGPT and Claude

    The Swedish government has barred employees from accessing browser-based versions of ChatGPT or Claude on their work computers over security concerns relating to the processing of sensitive data. "Officials were concerned that entering sensitive information into these models without an agreement setting out how to protect and secure the data could lead to it being fed into the model and stored for training," Euro News reported.

  17. 42 repositories hijacked
    42 Hijacked GitHub Repositories Armed With npm Supply-Chain Payloads

    JFrog and SafeDep have uncovered a campaign in which threat actors hijacked third-party 42 GitHub repositories across 11 owners to deploy payload blobs large enough "to evade the GitHub search and API paths normally used to find this kind of compromise." JFrog said, "The repositories contain execution hooks for AI coding assistants and IDEs, plus 12.9 to 13.7 MB polymorphic wrappers that all decode to the same hidden CI-publisher payload." The activity is assessed to be related to a Miasma-family npm worm propagated under various packages ending with "testmetest." According to SafeDep, the worm "shares code with Miasma 'Phantom Gyp' from June 2026 and adds the token-revocation wiper from Mini Shai-Hulud. The malicious versions steal credentials, spread to other packages and repositories, and install a wiper that deletes the home directory when the victim revokes the stolen GitHub token." Unsuspecting developers who installed the packages had their data stolen and repositories compromised with malicious code to produce further malicious testmetest releases and run shellpanel workflows targeting cPanel systems through CVE-2026-41940, overlapping with a prior campaign detailed by Socket in July 2026.

  18. Android banking malware-as-a-service
    MR ROBOT, a MaaS Operation Targeting Indian Bank Customers

    A new Android malware operation called MR ROBOT is targeting customers of Indian banks and transforming banking fraud into a subscription business, with cybercriminals renting customized banking trojans to steal OTPs, card details, UPI PINs and credentials while secretly forwarding calls to bypass security checks. "It is not a single-actor campaign but a rented crimeware platform: a master operator leases access to affiliates, who use a Telegram bot ('APK Shield) and a web control panel (v7.0) to build personalized banking trojans on demand and distribute them through fake Play-Store-style pages and messaging-app lures," CloudSEK said. The kit impersonates around 36 lure apps, including banks, utility providers, and government services. One affiliate is estimated to have intercepted 5407 text messages from 153 infected devices.

  19. MDM platforms abused for remote access
    Attackers Abuse Hexnode and Rippling MDM to Deploy Persistent Remote Access

    Threat actors are abusing legitimate mobile device management (MDM) platforms, like Hexnode and Rippling, by using social engineering to enroll devices or install management agents, per Huntress. "Once established, MDM provides a trusted, privileged path for malicious activity, such as deploying rogue RMM tools and maintaining remote access," it said.

  20. Critical Gotenberg RCE exploited
    Attackers Exploit Gotenberg RCE Flaw to Deploy Custom Go Reverse Shell

    Threat actors are exploiting CVE-2026-42589 (CVSS score: 9.8), a critical remote code execution flaw in Gotenberg, to deliver a Go-based reverse shell called "cache_base." The flaw was patched in May 2026. According to VulnCheck, the activity originated from a residential Japanese IP address in early October 2026. "The execution flow is straightforward: acquire a lock, collect host information, connect to C2, register the victim, and open a shell," VulnCheck said. Over the past 30 days, the vulnerability has recorded 1,358 exploitation events from 128 unique source IP addresses.

  21. Discord discussions go public
    Discord Plans to Put Messages From Discoverable Servers in Web Search

    Discord has announced it will allow search engines to index discussions in Discoverable Servers and make them accessible on the web to users outside the platform without an account or invitation, starting mid-December 2026. "Discussions in Discoverable Servers will soon be easier to find when you search the web, so you can find the answer you're looking for and step straight into the conversation on Discord," it said. The changes apply only to Discoverable Servers and do not extend to private servers and direct messages.

  22. 800+ ransomware victims claimed
    The Gentlemen RaaS Detailed

    The Gentlemen ransomware operation has claimed more than 800 victims across multiple regions and sectors, with most attacks targeting organizations in the U.S. and Europe. "The group supports multiple platforms, with ransomware variants targeting Windows, Linux, NAS, and BSD systems, allowing its affiliates to target a broad range of enterprise environments," Acronis said. "The group's operations include the use of EDR-killing tools. In a recent incident, a custom dropper was observed deploying vulnerable Safetica ProcessMonitorDriver [CVE-2025-70795] and Lenovo BootRepair.sys drivers to terminate security processes."

  23. AI model loading RCE risk
    Arbitrary Code Execution in Unsloth's Model Loader

    Pillar Security has disclosed an arbitrary-code-execution vulnerability in Unsloth's core model-loading path (CVE-2026-93348, CVSS score: 8.6). It has been fixed in unsloth_zoo 2026.8.14. "An attacker-controlled model configuration could cause Python code to execute during loading," researcher Ariel Fogel said. "The affected code ran inside the model-loading process, with access to whatever that process could read, modify, or authenticate to. In an AI development environment, that can include proprietary datasets, model artifacts, Hugging Face tokens, and cloud credentials. Exploitation required an affected loading path to process an attacker-controlled configuration."

  24. Unauthenticated root-level RCE
    Critical RCE in an EAC Voting Resource Calculator

    XBOW said it identified an unauthenticated, critical-severity remote code execution bug in a public web application belonging to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission (EAC). "The vulnerable application was a resource/logistics calculator, not a voting machine or voter registration system," XBOW researcher Ariel Walter Garcia said. "The flaw allowed an unauthenticated attacker to execute code as root inside the backend container, with access to locally protected resources and outbound network connectivity, a privileged foothold reachable via a crafted unauthenticated web request."

  25. Session-hijacking RAT emerges
    New DataCore RAT Emerges

    A new remote access trojan called DarkCore comes with a dedicated browser that could let attackers access Gmail, WhatsApp, and MediaFire accounts using stolen sessions, while giving the impression that the activity is originating from the victim's own IP address. DarkCore was first advertised on cybercrime forums in August 2026. "The seller describes a browser that reuses those sessions to access work mailboxes, instant messaging apps, cloud storage and other services through the infected machine's IP address," BlackFog said. "The purpose is to make the access look like legitimate activity from the user."

  26. AI-powered malware framework
    NIK C2, an AI-enabled C2 Framework

    Cisco Talos has disclosed details of a new AI-integrated command-and-control (C2) framework called NIK C2. The implant features surveillance, theft, lateral movement, and evasion capabilities, including credential dumping, RDP session hijacking, process hollowing, and a C2-driven screen lock ransomware module. "NIK C2 contains a Windows implant, using which, an actor can dump credentials, stream the victim's keystrokes to collect the targeted victim's sensitive data, and instruct an integrated AI model to analyze the harvested data, all within the compromised session," Talos said. "In this framework, the actor has abused the OpenAI Chat Completions application programming interface (API), which is an HTTP endpoint that enables ChatGPT-style conversations programmatically. In addition to the features that enable theft, an actor can also deploy desktop screen-locking ransomware via the NIK C2 implant onto the victim machine, leading to a ransom demand in Bitcoin or USDT cryptocurrencies." Three different versions of the malware have been identified to date since August 12, 2026. Talos said NIK C2 alters adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session.

  27. Malicious PDF delivers backdoor
    Fake FedEx Invoice Leads to Sirius Backdoor

    A phishing email using a FedEx tax invoice lure and containing a ZIP archive with a PDF has been observed triggering a multi-stage infection process to deliver a previously undocumented variant of the Sirius Backdoor. "The PDF abuses /OpenAction and /Launch objects to trigger an embedded Base64-encoded PowerShell command upon opening," Trellix said. "Execution relies on social engineering to trick the user into approving the PDF reader's security confirmation prompt. The PowerShell stager decrypts and reflectively loads a .NET assembly in memory. This loader performs process hollowing into legitimate Windows processes such as msbuild.exe, svchost.exe, etc., allowing the malware to operate under trusted process contexts." The final payload is SIRIUS, a Microsoft Visual C++ based backdoor with extended remote access capabilities.

  28. AI reshapes ransomware economics
    New Economics of Ransomware and Extortion

    A new analysis from Flare has revealed that threat actors are building a mixed AI toolkit, combining commercial models with local, open-weight, and jailbroken alternatives, as well as leaning on stolen AI credentials to shift costs to victims. "Where AI can help is with understanding systems, writing tools and troubleshooting. The threat actor still needs access, decisions and a way to obtain payment," Flare said. "If AI helps an affiliate write a working data-export script without hiring a specialist, the affiliate may avoid that specialist’s fee and the wait for their help. AI makes expertise cheaper to obtain only when the cost of using and checking its work is lower than the cost of the specialist help it replaces."

  29. Emerging data-extortion threat
    ScarlettGroup, an Emerging Data-Extortion Actor

    A recently observed cyber-extortion actor named ScarlettGroup is publicly advertising alleged data compromises and uses negotiation deadlines and threatened disclosures to pressure targeted organizations. The group's dark web site listing includes victims from technology, education, government, and entertainment sectors. "ScarlettGroup demonstrates characteristics associated with financially motivated data-extortion operations, including public victim claims, deadline-based pressure, and underground forum activity," Foresiet said. "Its dedicated leak-site infrastructure and structured disclosure mechanism indicate an organized approach to promoting alleged compromises and exerting reputational pressure."

  30. Infostealers evolve into RATs
    StealC Returns as Stadia RAT

    Following its disruption in June 2026 as part of Operation Endgame, StealC has returned four months later as Stadia. "This time it's not a stealer: it's a full remote access trojan," Varonis said. "The RAT's features include hidden desktop control, a live command shell, a file explorer, a process manager and an in-memory loader, with StealC's stealer welded on as one module among six. The actor behind Stadia is working hard to win back original StealC customers: every former StealC customer is offered a free month on the top ($900) tier." The development comes as Moonlock Lab revealed that the Icarus macOS stealer has similarly evolved from a smash-and-grab crypto and data stealer to a malware with remote-access capabilities. The new iteration is called ICMacOS. "The stealer is actively advertised on cybercrime forums by a Russian-speaking actor operating under the handle GlowComa, with feature updates regularly announced via Telegram," SOCRadar said. "GlowComa promotes ICMacOS alongside Icarus ClickFix, a companion panel designed to deliver payloads using malicious copy-and-paste terminal commands. The infection chain relies on initial dropper scripts to detect the host architecture and harvest administrator passwords using fake system dialogs before delivering the primary payload." Another macOS-focused stealer is Aokigahara, which goes beyond browsers, VPN clients, cryptocurrency wallets, FTP/SFTP clients, password managers, and email applications to also target AI applications and development tools. "The stealer collects authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and other tools," Check Point said. "Stolen AI credentials could offer opportunities for monetization. Usable credentials or session tokens could enable unauthorized access to paid AI services or the resale of compromised accounts."

That's the week's mess. Some attacks were clever, some were painfully simple, and a few attackers made life easier for the people investigating them. The common problem? Too much trust in things nobody was watching closely.

AI is adding new tricks, but the old ones aren't going anywhere. Stolen credentials, weak access controls, and forgotten bugs still get plenty of work done. New tools, familiar mistakes.

The useful part is knowing where those mistakes keep showing up. That's usually where the next problem starts.

"The malicious scanner runs from a major cloud provider and rotates through about 32 AI bot identities, spanning crawlers and assistants from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Perplexity, and others," Will Glazier said. "It ignores web pages and requests files that commonly store secrets, including .env configuration files, cloud credential files, private SSH keys, and server environment data, working from a list of roughly 90 file paths. Each address sends a short burst of 50 to 190 requests in about eight seconds and then moves on. The scanner works through targets one at a time, around the clock, and first sends random nonsense paths to find websites that answer every request, a common scanning technique. It hit organizations in financial services, retail, telecommunications, energy, and software, and stayed active from at least late September through late October."

  10. China-linked network intrusion
    China-Linked Attacker Breached a Fiji Organization

    The U.S. Embassy in Fiji has revealed that hackers linked to China broke into a regional organization based in Suva between July and August 2026. "Hackers with links to China maintained access to the organization's network over several days," it said. The embassy did not name the threat actor. Nor did it disclose what data the attackers may have accessed.

  11. Camera software weaponized
    Attackers Weaponize Camera Management Software

    Attackers have been breaking into enterprise networks via camera management software, according to new research from security firm Huntress, which observed multiple incidents in September and October 2026 and traced them back to a compromised application. Source code artifacts point to a Korean company selling analog and IP cameras and digital and network video recorders. The activity abuses the legitimate "WpcMon.exe" binary to sideload DLLs that establish outbound connections to a remote server. "This activity demonstrates how attackers can blend malicious code with trusted Windows components to evade detection," Huntress said.

  12. 68 GB government data breach
    68 GB Data Stolen from a Philippine Government Agency

    In a major operational security blunder, an unknown threat actor stole 68 GB from a Philippine government agency, maintained a detailed log of the transfer, then left that log open on the internet at 13.163.205[.]35:80. "The copy finished in under 24 minutes on September 6, 2026," Hunt.io said. "The transfer log records 27 SQL Server backups whose filenames correspond to the case-management systems of a Philippine overseas-employment and migrant-worker administration. Beside the log sat the operator's toolkit, a rebranded GodPotato build, a PowerShell stager, two payloads and a full Impacket environment."

  13. AI model data exfiltration concerns
    Cohere Says Alibaba's Qwen Model Tried to Send a File to China

    Canadian AI company Cohere has claimed that it caught Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model unsuccessfully attempting to send data to China from its evaluation sandbox as part of a prompt instructing the LLM to detect malicious file download and execution by monitoring for curl processes downloading bash scripts to /tmp followed by bash execution. "Asked to write a defensive detection rule, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ignored instructions and inventoried the machine it was running on and then tried to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing," Cohere said. "We cannot answer whether this is deliberate or a leftover glitch from training." Cohere has also released a dataset containing the model trace and corresponding raw token IDs in connection with the behavior. "The exact output is not guaranteed all the time, and many trials may be required to reproduce the behavior," Cohere said, adding "there are similarly unexpected URLs that the model also tends to output, most containing aliyunc." However, the findings have also led to social media chatter that the company is resorting to geopolitical fearmongering and that they are an attempt to clamp down on open-weights models.

  14. Post-quantum migration roadmap
    NIST Releases Guidance for Post-Quantum Cryptography Transition

    The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has released guidelines that detail the timelines for transitioning away from quantum-vulnerable algorithms to quantum-resistant standards. "The report describes different use cases and says why one migration might take longer than another," said NIST mathematician Dustin Moody, who heads the PQC standardization project. "We understand there's not one strategy that fits all use cases, and we want to help people handle their migration while staying abreast of what's changing."

  15. AI-powered ransomware operation exposed
    n0n Ransomware Linked to AI-Assisted Extortion Operation

    SOCRadar has uncovered the live workspace (i.e., open directory) of a threat actor tied to the n0n ransomware group, which exposed the operation's full workflow as of September 2026. The directory at 185.157.161[.]148 includes an AI coding agent configured with about 150 models to produce hundreds of attack scripts, with more than $7,216 in usage costs. "Entry points included a credential stuffing campaign against 305 FortiGate SSL-VPN devices, exposed AWS keys, weak RDP/WinRM credentials, and compromised hosting management portals," SOCRadar said. At least 23 organizations across 14 countries are said to have been identified in the workspace, including a U.S. sports retailer, a cloud provider, a teachers’ union, a Venezuelan ISP, an Argentine ministry and a pharmaceutical subsidiary.

  16. Government AI access restricted
    Sweden Blocks Government Access to ChatGPT and Claude

    The Swedish government has barred employees from accessing browser-based versions of ChatGPT or Claude on their work computers over security concerns relating to the processing of sensitive data. "Officials were concerned that entering sensitive information into these models without an agreement setting out how to protect and secure the data could lead to it being fed into the model and stored for training," Euro News reported.

  17. 42 repositories hijacked
    42 Hijacked GitHub Repositories Armed With npm Supply-Chain Payloads

    JFrog and SafeDep have uncovered a campaign in which threat actors hijacked third-party 42 GitHub repositories across 11 owners to deploy payload blobs large enough "to evade the GitHub search and API paths normally used to find this kind of compromise." JFrog said, "The repositories contain execution hooks for AI coding assistants and IDEs, plus 12.9 to 13.7 MB polymorphic wrappers that all decode to the same hidden CI-publisher payload." The activity is assessed to be related to a Miasma-family npm worm propagated under various packages ending with "testmetest." According to SafeDep, the worm "shares code with Miasma 'Phantom Gyp' from June 2026 and adds the token-revocation wiper from Mini Shai-Hulud. The malicious versions steal credentials, spread to other packages and repositories, and install a wiper that deletes the home directory when the victim revokes the stolen GitHub token." Unsuspecting developers who installed the packages had their data stolen and repositories compromised with malicious code to produce further malicious testmetest releases and run shellpanel workflows targeting cPanel systems through CVE-2026-41940, overlapping with a prior campaign detailed by Socket in July 2026.

  18. Android banking malware-as-a-service
    MR ROBOT, a MaaS Operation Targeting Indian Bank Customers

    A new Android malware operation called MR ROBOT is targeting customers of Indian banks and transforming banking fraud into a subscription business, with cybercriminals renting customized banking trojans to steal OTPs, card details, UPI PINs and credentials while secretly forwarding calls to bypass security checks. "It is not a single-actor campaign but a rented crimeware platform: a master operator leases access to affiliates, who use a Telegram bot ('APK Shield) and a web control panel (v7.0) to build personalized banking trojans on demand and distribute them through fake Play-Store-style pages and messaging-app lures," CloudSEK said. The kit impersonates around 36 lure apps, including banks, utility providers, and government services. One affiliate is estimated to have intercepted 5407 text messages from 153 infected devices.

  19. MDM platforms abused for remote access
    Attackers Abuse Hexnode and Rippling MDM to Deploy Persistent Remote Access

    Threat actors are abusing legitimate mobile device management (MDM) platforms, like Hexnode and Rippling, by using social engineering to enroll devices or install management agents, per Huntress. "Once established, MDM provides a trusted, privileged path for malicious activity, such as deploying rogue RMM tools and maintaining remote access," it said.

  20. Critical Gotenberg RCE exploited
    Attackers Exploit Gotenberg RCE Flaw to Deploy Custom Go Reverse Shell

    Threat actors are exploiting CVE-2026-42589 (CVSS score: 9.8), a critical remote code execution flaw in Gotenberg, to deliver a Go-based reverse shell called "cache_base." The flaw was patched in May 2026. According to VulnCheck, the activity originated from a residential Japanese IP address in early October 2026. "The execution flow is straightforward: acquire a lock, collect host information, connect to C2, register the victim, and open a shell," VulnCheck said. Over the past 30 days, the vulnerability has recorded 1,358 exploitation events from 128 unique source IP addresses.

  21. Discord discussions go public
    Discord Plans to Put Messages From Discoverable Servers in Web Search

    Discord has announced it will allow search engines to index discussions in Discoverable Servers and make them accessible on the web to users outside the platform without an account or invitation, starting mid-December 2026. "Discussions in Discoverable Servers will soon be easier to find when you search the web, so you can find the answer you're looking for and step straight into the conversation on Discord," it said. The changes apply only to Discoverable Servers and do not extend to private servers and direct messages.

  22. 800+ ransomware victims claimed
    The Gentlemen RaaS Detailed

    The Gentlemen ransomware operation has claimed more than 800 victims across multiple regions and sectors, with most attacks targeting organizations in the U.S. and Europe. "The group supports multiple platforms, with ransomware variants targeting Windows, Linux, NAS, and BSD systems, allowing its affiliates to target a broad range of enterprise environments," Acronis said. "The group's operations include the use of EDR-killing tools. In a recent incident, a custom dropper was observed deploying vulnerable Safetica ProcessMonitorDriver [CVE-2025-70795] and Lenovo BootRepair.sys drivers to terminate security processes."

  23. AI model loading RCE risk
    Arbitrary Code Execution in Unsloth's Model Loader

    Pillar Security has disclosed an arbitrary-code-execution vulnerability in Unsloth's core model-loading path (CVE-2026-93348, CVSS score: 8.6). It has been fixed in unsloth_zoo 2026.8.14. "An attacker-controlled model configuration could cause Python code to execute during loading," researcher Ariel Fogel said. "The affected code ran inside the model-loading process, with access to whatever that process could read, modify, or authenticate to. In an AI development environment, that can include proprietary datasets, model artifacts, Hugging Face tokens, and cloud credentials. Exploitation required an affected loading path to process an attacker-controlled configuration."

  24. Unauthenticated root-level RCE
    Critical RCE in an EAC Voting Resource Calculator

    XBOW said it identified an unauthenticated, critical-severity remote code execution bug in a public web application belonging to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission (EAC). "The vulnerable application was a resource/logistics calculator, not a voting machine or voter registration system," XBOW researcher Ariel Walter Garcia said. "The flaw allowed an unauthenticated attacker to execute code as root inside the backend container, with access to locally protected resources and outbound network connectivity, a privileged foothold reachable via a crafted unauthenticated web request."

  25. Session-hijacking RAT emerges
    New DataCore RAT Emerges

    A new remote access trojan called DarkCore comes with a dedicated browser that could let attackers access Gmail, WhatsApp, and MediaFire accounts using stolen sessions, while giving the impression that the activity is originating from the victim's own IP address. DarkCore was first advertised on cybercrime forums in August 2026. "The seller describes a browser that reuses those sessions to access work mailboxes, instant messaging apps, cloud storage and other services through the infected machine's IP address," BlackFog said. "The purpose is to make the access look like legitimate activity from the user."

  26. AI-powered malware framework
    NIK C2, an AI-enabled C2 Framework

    Cisco Talos has disclosed details of a new AI-integrated command-and-control (C2) framework called NIK C2. The implant features surveillance, theft, lateral movement, and evasion capabilities, including credential dumping, RDP session hijacking, process hollowing, and a C2-driven screen lock ransomware module. "In this framework, the actor has abused the OpenAI Chat Completions application programming interface (API), which is an HTTP endpoint that enables ChatGPT-style conversations programmatically. In addition to the features that enable theft, an actor can also deploy desktop screen-locking ransomware via the NIK C2 implant onto the victim machine, leading to a ransom demand in Bitcoin or USDT cryptocurrencies." Three different versions of the malware have been identified to date since August 12, 2026. Talos said NIK C2 alters adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session.

  27. Malicious PDF delivers backdoor
    Fake FedEx Invoice Leads to Sirius Backdoor

    A phishing email using a FedEx tax invoice lure and containing a ZIP archive with a PDF has been observed triggering a multi-stage infection process to deliver a previously undocumented variant of the Sirius Backdoor. "The PDF abuses /OpenAction and /Launch objects to trigger an embedded Base64-encoded PowerShell command upon opening," Trellix said. "Execution relies on social engineering to trick the user into approving the PDF reader's security confirmation prompt. The PowerShell stager decrypts and reflectively loads a .NET assembly in memory. This loader performs process hollowing into legitimate Windows processes such as msbuild.exe, svchost.exe, etc., allowing the malware to operate under trusted process contexts." The final payload is SIRIUS, a Microsoft Visual C++ based backdoor with extended remote access capabilities.

  28. AI reshapes ransomware economics
    New Economics of Ransomware and Extortion

    A new analysis from Flare has revealed that threat actors are building a mixed AI toolkit, combining commercial models with local, open-weight, and jailbroken alternatives, as well as leaning on stolen AI credentials to shift costs to victims. "Where AI can help is with understanding systems, writing tools and troubleshooting. The threat actor still needs access, decisions and a way to obtain payment," Flare said. "If AI helps an affiliate write a working data-export script without hiring a specialist, the affiliate may avoid that specialist’s fee and the wait for their help.   29. Emerging data-extortion threat

    A recently observed cyber-extortion actor named ScarlettGroup is publicly advertising alleged data compromises and uses negotiation deadlines and threatened disclosures to pressure targeted organizations. The group's dark web site listing includes victims from technology, education, government, and entertainment sectors. "ScarlettGroup demonstrates characteristics associated with financially motivated data-extortion operations, including public victim claims, deadline-based pressure, and underground forum activity," Foresiet said. "Its dedicated leak-site infrastructure and structured disclosure mechanism indicate an organized approach to promoting alleged compromises and exerting reputational pressure."

  30. Infostealers evolve into RATs

    Following its disruption in June 2026 as part of Operation Endgame, StealC has returned four months later as Stadia. "This time it's not a stealer: it's a full remote access trojan," Varonis said. "The RAT's features include hidden desktop control, a live command shell, a file explorer, a process manager and an in-memory loader, with StealC's stealer welded on as one module among six. The actor behind Stadia is working hard to win back original StealC customers: every former StealC customer is offered a free month on the top ($900) tier." The development comes as Moonlock Lab revealed that the Icarus macOS stealer has similarly evolved from a smash-and-grab crypto and data stealer to a malware with remote-access capabilities. "The stealer is actively advertised on cybercrime forums by a Russian-speaking actor operating under the handle GlowComa, with feature updates regularly announced via Telegram," SOCRadar said. "GlowComa promotes ICMacOS alongside Icarus ClickFix, a companion panel designed to deliver payloads using malicious copy-and-paste terminal commands. The infection chain relies on initial dropper scripts to detect the host architecture and harvest administrator passwords using fake system dialogs before delivering the primary payload." Another macOS-focused stealer is Aokigahara, which goes beyond browsers, VPN clients, cryptocurrency wallets, FTP/SFTP clients, password managers, and email applications to also target AI applications and development tools. "The stealer collects authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and other tools," Check Point said. "Stolen AI credentials could offer opportunities for monetization. Usable credentials or session tokens could enable unauthorized access to paid AI services or the resale of compromised accounts."

The useful part is knowing where those mistakes keep showing up. That's usually where the next problem starts.

item.title: Binance Suffers Security Breach Affecting $6.3 Billion in Assets, Nearly $3 Billion Frozen (2026)
item.description:
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that a "security incident" on its platform has impacted about $6.3 billion worth of assets.

The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange said nearly $3 billion of those assets have been frozen on-chain so far. 

Tether and Circle said they have frozen more than 1.567 billion USDT and 800 million USDC related to the incident, respectively. The Arbitrum Security Council is said to have executed a transaction to freeze about $30.5 million from the Binance Exploit. 

"Initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions," Binance said in an update.

The company said there is no evidence of a wallet private key leak, adding it will cover all losses from the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) fund and its own funds.

Out of an abundance of caution, Binance has also taken the following steps -

  • Temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed
  • Revoked the affected address authorization;
  • Engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds

"We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice," Binance said.

In an update, Binance said it expects withdrawals to resume in 48 hours, after its team "completes a security revamp of the withdrawal service and its related addresses."

The development makes it the biggest cryptocurrency heist recorded to date, surpassing the theft of about $1.5 billion from Bybit in February 2025. The incident was subsequently attributed to North Korea.

"Our current estimate on the amount stolen is approximately $5.912 billion at time of theft, nearly 4x the amount stolen in the next largest crypto heist," blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis said in an X post.

Attributed to North Korea's TraderTraitor

TRM Labs has attributed the record-breaking hack targeting Binance to threat actors from North Korea with high confidence. The blockchain analytics company linked it to TraderTraitor, which was also behind the 2025 Bybit heist, based on what it said were "robust on and off-chain intelligence sources."

"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," TRM Labs said.

"The laundering observed so far, built on large swaps through market makers and lending protocols, differs from the bridge-heavy pattern that followed Bybit."

TRM Labs said preparation for the attack was underway at least 36 hours before the theft, with the attackers taking over a Binance hot wallet to send its "entire balance to an attacker-controlled address" -

At 20:20 UTC, the operator submitted a single transaction containing 50 authorizations. Each was signed by the Binance hot wallet, and each pointed it to a sweeper contract that accepts instructions only from the operator. Every wallet keeps a running count of its transactions, called a nonce, and an authorization works only at the count the wallet has reached at the moment it executes. The Binance hot wallet processes a steady flow of withdrawals, so its count keeps moving forward. By preparing signatures for 50 consecutive counts, the attacker guaranteed that one would still be valid when the transaction executed. One matched, which was all the attacker needed. The signatures were produced in advance as a batch.

Three minutes and 24 seconds after the delegation, the operator instructed the Binance hot wallet to send its entire balance to an attacker-controlled address. That single transaction moved 167,464 ETH and 63 tokens, including 1.615 billion USDT.

The most likely explanation is that the attacker gained the ability to make Binance's hot wallet signing system sign transactions of its choosing across chains. The batch of 50 pre-signed authorizations suggests the access may have been limited in time, or that signatures had to be requested through a system. Binance has yet to publish a root cause.

Chainalysis has also linked the hack to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) with a high degree of confidence, stating it "observed funds stolen by DPRK in last month's Bitget exploit commingling with funds stolen from Binance."

"The ability to quickly identify and understand illicit activity is increasingly important as North Korea increasingly uses sophisticated automation to move and obscure stolen funds," the company noted earlier this month. "Investigators must keep pace with these tactics while applying the judgment and expertise needed to make sense of complex on-chain activity."

So far, Tether, Circle, Ripple, and World Liberty Financial have frozen about $2.67 billion in stablecoins, and Arbitrum's Security Council has frozen about $30 million in ETH and ARB. The attacker continues to retain control of more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth about $2.4 billion, plus smaller amounts on other chains.

Elliptic's chief scientist and founder, Dr. Tom Robinson, told The Hacker News that cryptocurrency assets with a total value of $6.43 billion were stolen from Binance, assessing North Korea-linked actors perpetrated the theft, citing similar tradecraft and co-mingling of funds from another hack attributed to them.

"Rather than stealing Binance's private keys, the attacker appears to have been able to get Binance's own systems to sign transactions on their behalf," Elliptic said.

"This closely resembles the Bybit theft, in which North Korean hackers compromised a developer's machine at the wallet provider Safe{Wallet} and manipulated the transaction that Bybit's signers approved. In both cases, it was the infrastructure and people around the wallets that were compromised, not the cryptography."

The company also noted that 2.84 billion of funds have been frozen, while the attacker is in control of around $3.33 billion of assets that cannot be frozen by an issuer and are spread across about 43 wallet addresses. This includes 511,861 ETH (1.15 billion), 18,270 BTC ($1.43 billion), 233 million XRP, and 670 million TRX.

The links to North Korea are based on the following factors -

  • Funds stolen from Binance and funds linked to the Bitget exploit have been sent to the same Ethereum address, 0x15104a9ce0f08a8f0075a0869ae80e795fe0feb7.
  • Attackers funded their wallet with three small Tornado Cash withdrawals, tested the attack code in advance, and executed pre-signed transactions in a single burst, similar to what was observed in Bybit and KelpDAO exploits.
  • The likely use of social engineering to trick employees into executing malware under the pretext of a coding test or a bogus project, a technique employed in DMM Bitcoin and Bybit hacks.

Despite these commonalities, Elliptic has urged caution in attributing the activity to North Korea, citing deviations from previously observed laundering patterns in terms of speed and methodology, as well as the absence of a root cause.

"DPRK launderers typically swap stolen stablecoins for native assets within minutes," Robinson said. "The attacker held the stolen USDT for 37 minutes on Ethereum and 46 minutes on Tron without converting most of it. North Korean-linked groups typically move funds faster and more efficiently. The use of market makers and DeFi lending protocols differs from the bridge-heavy laundering seen after the Bybit hack."

Chainalysis has also concurred with this assessment, stating it's observing never-seen-before laundering patterns with the stolen funds from the Binance exploit.

"Thousands of transactions in a short period suggest that the attackers are using automation to obscure the trail of funds," it said. "Rather than simply moving funds onward, they repeatedly circulate them among addresses, often sending funds back to addresses involved earlier in the sequence."

"Many addresses follow a consistent pattern: they receive exactly 1 TRX, then receive additional funds, then forward funds to other addresses. This repeated sequence suggests a programmatic process for moving and redistributing the stolen funds."

When asked if there were any indicators that could have helped identify and prevent this attack beforehand, Robinson said it was possible only in hindsight.

"The day before the attack, the attacker funded their wallet through the Tornado Cash mixer," Robinson added. "A few hours before, they tested their code on three wallets. None of this would have stood out at the time."

Assuming the Binance hack was orchestrated by North Korea, the development once again signals how the threat actors continue to operate with impunity despite continued law enforcement efforts and sanctions pressure.

"The rewards are huge and the risks to them are small," Robinson said. "The hackers are beyond the reach of law enforcement. North Korea is already heavily sanctioned, and crypto theft is one of the few ways it can still raise billions."

"They target people rather than technology, through fake job offers and malware, and it only takes one compromised laptop. They then launder the funds through mixers, bridges and OTC brokers, mostly out of reach of Western law enforcement. "However, tracing and freezing have improved, which makes each theft less profitable."

Binance has since revealed that its ongoing investigation has "uncovered additional points of breach" that goes beyond the compromised laptop, and that it's "doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it."

The company has also disclosed that it's "recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms, and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds."

"Our initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said. "That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions."

"To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual."

Investigation Remains Ongoing

In a new recovery update shared late Friday, Binance said it's working with internal and external security experts to lay out the entire attack sequence, identify all contributing factors, and determine the appropriate measures to prevent such incidents from happening again.

The company also said it has undertaken the following steps -

  • Contained the compromised infrastructure, revoked affected authorizations, and implemented additional controls to prevent further unauthorized activity.
  • Traced and frozen approximately $3 billion on-chain to date, with more recovery efforts to follow.
  • Strengthened security checks across affected infrastructure.
  • Temporarily suspended withdrawals while conducting additional security reviews, implementing remediation measures and validating the integrity of affected systems.
  • Continued working to restore withdrawal services safely.

"We take full responsibility for addressing this security incident, strengthening our security infrastructure, and ensuring our users are protected," it said.

In a post shared on LinkedIn, Cynthia Kaiser, senior vice president of the Halcyon Ransomware Research Center and the former Deputy Director of the FBI's Cyber Division, said that manipulating people and trust continues to be the most effective method to obtain access to target networks. 

"There are no 'North Korean criminal hackers,'" Kaiser said. "They are all 'North Korean state hackers' and this theft is a national security issue not just a financial crime."

TraderTraitor exemplifies this modus operandi by comprising software developer or engineers' workstation, and then abusing that access to perform reconnaissance and develop the technical attack to steal steal cryptocurrency from the victim organization using rapid, coordinated transactions, Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat research at Sophos, said.

"This group are experts at mapping out the technical and business processes necessary to make authorized transfers and develop a custom attack tailored to the victim," Pilling told The Hacker News.

"This group in particular are somewhat artists in terms of getting into these distributed finance companies. TraderTraitor focus on large operations. In the past, they’ve developed their own fake applications and tried to use those to get inside organizations."

(The story has been updated after publication to reflect the latest developments and additional insights from Elliptic.)

"The ability to quickly identify and understand illicit activity is increasingly important as North Korea increasingly uses sophisticated automation to move and obscure stolen funds," the company noted earlier this month. "Investigators must keep pace with these tactics while applying the judgment and expertise needed to make sense of complex on-chain activity."
